misconceptions.statement: All vitamins dissolve in water, so all can be washed out in cooking.
misconceptions.why: Students generalise from vitamin C and B being in fruit juices and soups.
misconceptions.fix: Vitamins A, D, E and K dissolve in fat, not water. Only B and C dissolve in water.

probe.question: Which vitamin is NOT easily lost into water when vegetables are boiled: vitamin A or vitamin C?
probe.wrong_answer: Both are lost equally because vitamins dissolve in water.

misconceptions.root_belief: what is true of some is true of all

misconceptions.statement: Vitamin B and vitamin C are the same vitamin.
misconceptions.why: Both are water-soluble and common in 'healthy food', and letters sound alike.
misconceptions.fix: B and C are different vitamins with different jobs and sources. Lack of B1 causes beriberi, lack of C causes scurvy.

probe.question: Will eating whole grains cure scurvy?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because grains have vitamins like B and C.

misconceptions.statement: Only oranges and lemons have vitamin C.
misconceptions.why: Textbooks and ads link vitamin C mainly with oranges.
misconceptions.fix: Amla, guava, tomato and many other fruits and vegetables also have vitamin C. Amla has more than oranges.

probe.question: Name a cheap Indian fruit rich in vitamin C other than citrus.
probe.wrong_answer: There is none; only oranges and lemons.

misconceptions.root_belief: one famous example is the only example

misconceptions.statement: Only sour-tasting foods contain vitamin C.
misconceptions.why: Lemon, amla and tamarind are sour, so taste seems the sign.
misconceptions.fix: Taste does not decide the vitamin. Some vitamin C foods like cabbage, green chilli and potato are not sour.

probe.question: Does sweet-tasting papaya or non-sour green chilli contain vitamin C?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because they are not sour.

misconceptions.root_belief: a visible property shows what is inside

misconceptions.statement: Carrots make eyesight perfect, so eating many carrots cures all eye problems.
misconceptions.why: Common sayings say carrots are good for eyes.
misconceptions.fix: Carrots give vitamin A which prevents night blindness. They do not cure other eye problems like needing spectacles.

probe.question: A child needs spectacles for blurred distant vision. Will eating carrots remove the need?

misconceptions.statement: Taking vitamin tablets or syrups is as good as eating healthy food, so a balanced diet is not needed.
misconceptions.why: Students see supplements advertised as complete nutrition and think food is only for energy, not for vitamins.
misconceptions.fix: Supplements cannot replace food. Food gives many nutrients together, along with carbohydrates, proteins, fats and fibre. Tablets are used only when a doctor advises.

probe.question: Ravi takes a vitamin tablet daily. Can he now skip vegetables, fruits and dal?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the tablet gives all he needs so he can skip them.

misconceptions.root_belief: Pills can fully substitute for natural food

misconceptions.statement: Deficiency diseases like scurvy and rickets spread from a sick person to others by touch or air.
misconceptions.why: Students link all diseases with germs and contagion, such as cold or chickenpox.
misconceptions.fix: Deficiency diseases are caused by lack of a nutrient in the diet over a long time. They are not caused by germs and do not spread from person to person.

probe.question: Should a child with rickets be kept away from classmates so they do not catch it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the classmates can catch rickets from the child.

misconceptions.root_belief: All diseases are caused by germs and spread
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's ideas of disease causation

misconceptions.statement: Vitamin D must be eaten in food because the body cannot make it.
misconceptions.why: Students learn vitamins are obtained from food and assume this holds for every vitamin.
misconceptions.fix: The skin makes vitamin D when sunlight falls on it. Milk, eggs and fish give additional vitamin D.

probe.question: A child eats well but never goes out in the sun. Where does the body normally make vitamin D?
probe.wrong_answer: The body cannot make it; it only comes from food.

misconceptions.root_belief: Every nutrient comes only from food

misconceptions.statement: Since iodine is a mineral the body needs, eating a lot of extra iodised salt is better for health.
misconceptions.why: Students think more of a good nutrient always means more benefit.
misconceptions.fix: The body needs only a tiny amount of iodine, but regularly every day. Too much salt is harmful, and a small amount of iodised salt is enough.

probe.question: Meena adds double salt to her food to get more iodine. Is this a good idea?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, more iodine means a healthier body.

misconceptions.root_belief: More of a nutrient is always better

misconceptions.statement: Goitre is caused by an infection of the neck or by lifting heavy things.
misconceptions.why: Students see the swelling in the neck and think of injury or infection, not diet.
misconceptions.fix: Goitre is a swelling in the neck caused by lack of iodine in the diet, which affects the thyroid gland. Iodised salt prevents it.

probe.question: A woman has a swollen neck from goitre. What is the main cause?
probe.wrong_answer: A germ infection or muscle strain in the neck.

misconceptions.root_belief: Visible symptom shows a local cause

misconceptions.statement: Boiling vegetables for a long time makes them safer and does not reduce their vitamins.
misconceptions.why: Students link cooking more with cleanliness and kill-germs ideas, and ignore nutrient loss.
misconceptions.fix: Water-soluble vitamins like vitamin C and B are lost by overcooking and by throwing away cooking water. Cook for a short time and use the water, e.g. in dal or soup.

probe.question: Sita boils spinach for a long time and pours away the water. Is the vitamin content the same?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the vitamins stay the same in the spinach.

misconceptions.statement: Polished white rice is healthier than brown or unpolished rice because it is cleaner and looks better.
misconceptions.why: Students judge healthiness by appearance and refinement.
misconceptions.fix: Polishing removes the outer layer of rice that contains vitamin B1. Eating mainly polished rice can cause beriberi. Whole grains and unpolished rice keep the vitamin.

probe.question: Which rice gives more vitamin B1: polished white rice or unpolished rice?
probe.wrong_answer: Polished white rice, because it is cleaner and refined.

misconceptions.root_belief: Refined and clean-looking food is more nutritious
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's food and nutrition ideas
